summary: Discusses the need to delegate the E.F.F.3.IP6.ARPA reverse DNS zone so reverse lookups work for 6bone addresses, and makes specific recommendations about the process. It is a best current practice document.

eli5.summary: Reverse lookups turn an address back into a name. This explains how to set up the phone book page needed so that old IPv6 test network addresses can be looked up too.

questions: why was ip6.int replaced by ip6.arpa
subtitle: Asks IANA to hand the reverse-DNS zone for 6bone addresses over to the 6bone itself.

tldr.problem: Reverse lookups for 6bone IPv6 test addresses had used IP6.INT, but users needed to move to IP6.ARPA while the 6bone was still running.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC asks IANA to delegate the E.F.F.3.IP6.ARPA domain to the 6bone, which then delegates names within it to the top level 6bone ISPs, matching the 3FFE::/16 address space.
tldr.outcome: The 6bone provides the service for itself so the Regional Internet Registries are relieved of the cost, and the IP6.ARPA authority can end the service when the planned 6bone termination date arrives.

today: RFC 3681 is a Best Current Practice, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text describes the 6bone as a temporary network with a planned termination date.

sections.title: The 6bone and Reverse DNS
sections.content:
The 6bone, whose address space was allocated by RFC 2471, had provided a network for IPv6 experimentation for seven years. Reverse lookups for its addresses had been done through IP6.INT, and it was now important that thousands of 6bone users could update their IPv6 software to use IP6.ARPA (RFC 3152).

The 6bone had a limited life. A phaseout plan was being discussed, and the RFC expects 2.5 to 3.5 more years of operation. During that time, IP6.ARPA reverse lookup service for the 3ffe::/16 address space is required.
sections.eli5: A test network needed its address-to-name lookups moved to the new official phone book, and it would only be around for a few more years.

sections.title: Who Runs the Zone
sections.content:
Discussions between the 6bone and Regional Internet Registry (RIR) communities considered having the RIRs perform the service. It was agreed at the San Francisco IETF meeting in March 2003 that it was more practical for the 6bone to provide the service for itself.

This relieves the RIRs of the costs, yet still lets the IP6.ARPA authority terminate the service when the planned 6bone termination date is reached, anticipated to be June 6, 2006. The 6bone operational community planned to add new inet6num attributes in the 6bone registry database so that top level address space holders can request delegation to their reverse path servers.
sections.eli5: Rather than make the big registries do extra work, the testing network looks after its own page, and the owners of the big book can close it when the test ends.

sections.title: The Request to IANA
sections.content: The memo requests that IANA delegate the E.F.F.3.IP6.ARPA domain to the 6bone, following instructions to be provided by the IAB. Names within the zone are then delegated further within the top level 6bone ISPs, known as pTLAs, in line with the delegation of 6bone 3FFE::/16 address space.
sections.eli5: It asks the official list keeper to give the testing network its own page, which the network then splits among its biggest members.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that DNS spoofing of address-to-name mapping has been exploited in IPv4, but concludes that delegating the E.F.F.3.IP6.ARPA zone creates no new threats to the security of the internet.
sections.eli5: Giving the testing network its own page does not open any new ways to trick people.

references.text: Hinden, R., Fink, R. and J. Postel, "IPv6 Testing Address Allocation", RFC 2471, December 1998.
Bush, R., "Delegation of IP6.ARPA", BCP 49, RFC 3152, August 2001.
